say.text: A 58-year-old man is found at laparoscopy to have a groin sac. It comes through the posterior wall of the canal, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
Which hernia is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ignore the names for a moment. Which hernia comes through the deep ring, lateral to the vessels, and which through the posterior wall, medial to them?
Yes. A direct hernia bulges through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
So the side of the vessels decides the route. The name only tells you the family.
Tempting: indirect is the commonest groin hernia, so it feels like the safe pick.
It fails here. An indirect sac enters through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. This sac is medial to them.
Direct is the one that passes through the posterior wall, medial to the vessels.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: a confident pick of 'indirect' is the one to test against the vessels.

say.text: Tempting: a femoral hernia is a groin lump, and a sac that sits medial can look like one.
It fails. A femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, not beside the vessels.
The sac here comes through the posterior wall, medial to the vessels, which is a direct inguinal hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at the route: a groin lump is not placed by its side alone.

say.text: Use the route, not the name. An indirect sac enters through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, then runs down the canal.
A direct sac bulges through the posterior wall in Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the vessels.
A femoral hernia is a different site, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
A 45-year-old woman has a groin lump. Her surgeon marks it against the pubic tubercle.
Where does a femoral hernia's neck lie?

choices.label: Above and medial to the tubercle
Below and lateral to the tubercle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the inguinal canal. Does its exit lie above the tubercle or below it?
Yes. A femoral hernia emerges below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to it, so the tubercle separates the two.
Tempting: an inguinal hernia does emerge above and medial to the tubercle, so a groin lump seems to copy that spot.
It fails. That is where the inguinal hernia emerges. The femoral neck lies below and lateral to the tubercle.
Check where the neck sits against the tubercle before you name the hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the inguinal position is the habit to break: femoral is the other side of the tubercle.

say.text: A 40-year-old woman has a groin lump, and her surgeon asks which hernia is the most common in women.
Which is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the exact word in the question: 'most common', not 'more common in one sex'. Which hernia leads overall?
Yes. Indirect inguinal hernia is the most common hernia in women, as it is in men and in children.
Inguinal hernia is far more common in men overall, so the female skew does not change the ranking.
Tempting: femoral hernia is relatively more common in women, so it sounds like the answer.
It fails. Relatively more common is not most common. Indirect inguinal still leads in women.
Read the qualifier 'relatively' before you rank anything.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: 'relatively' in a 'most common' stem is the trap.

say.text: The vessels split the canal hernias: indirect lateral, direct medial.
The pubic tubercle splits inguinal from femoral, and the qualifier decides the most common.
